idiom_name: class with #private sealed map + node:crypto/WebCrypto sealing + toJSON()/inspect hooks
implementation_notes: TypeScript types erase at runtime, so private and readonly members protect nothing: the realization is the JavaScript one plus a typed surface - a class whose protected map lives in a #private field, sealed with an AEAD (node:crypto createCipheriv('aes-256-gcm') on the server, crypto.subtle.encrypt in the browser), with toJSON() and the Node inspect symbol controlling every rendering path and an exported interface describing the sealed view. What replaces the classic structure: the #private field plus the serialization hooks replace the classic TO's protected map and masked list, and the type system's contribution is limited to making the sealed/plaintext distinction visible in the API (a brand type, a reveal() signature) - never to enforcing it.
pitfalls: TypeScript's private/readonly erase at compile time: only ECMAScript #private fields are enforced at runtime, so anything that must stay hidden cannot be an ordinary property, however it is declared.

toJSON is called by JSON.stringify but not by spread, structuredClone, Object.assign or libraries that copy own properties, and console.log uses the runtime's inspect - all paths must be handled or the masked map leaks through one of them.

WebCrypto is asynchronous and absent from some bundled/edge runtimes, so a synchronous log or serialization path cannot use crypto.subtle; keep the crypto behind an interface and inject the implementation per runtime.

Compiled output and source maps expose field names and shapes, and decorator metadata can serialize more than intended: the requirement is to protect the values, but review what else ends up on the wire.
